CausalChain: Heavy alcohol consumption -> Disruption of gut microbiota with reduction of butyrate-producing bacteria -> Impaired intestinal barrier integrity -> Increased translocation of LPS and other endotoxins -> Activation of Kupffer cells and elevation of inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF) -> Enhanced oxidative stress via CYP2E1-mediated metabolism -> DNA adduct formation and genomic instability -> Promotion of hepatocarcinogenesis; Additionally, risk is magnified by PNPLA3 and other genetic variants.
Hypothesis: Restoration of butyrate-producing gut bacteria through probiotic or dietary interventions in patients with alcohol-associated cirrhosis will reduce LPS-mediated inflammatory signaling and oxidative DNA damage pathways, thereby lowering the incidence or progression of alcohol-associated hepatocellular carcinoma, especially in individuals carrying high-risk genetic polymorphisms such as PNPLA3.
Abstract: Alcohol‐associated liver disease (ALD) and its progression to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) are multifactorial processes involving both direct hepatocellular injury and extrahepatic modulators. A growing body of evidence indicates that alcohol‐induced gut microbial dysbiosis, characterized particularly by a loss of butyrate-producing bacteria, contributes to impaired gut barrier function and increased translocation of endotoxins. These, in turn, activate Kupffer cells and induce proinflammatory cytokines, thereby synergizing with oxidative stress generated via CYP2E1-mediated alcohol metabolism to drive DNA damage and hepatocarcinogenesis. Notably, genetic predispositions such as PNPLA3 variants further enhance individual risk. We present a novel hypothesis that targeted restoration of butyrate-producing gut microbiota may mitigate inflammatory and oxidative pathways and thereby reduce the risk of HCC in patients with alcohol-associated cirrhosis, particularly in those harboring high-risk genetic variants.
